Doer of the Word
DOO-er uhv thuh wurd
doctrinal phrase
From doer (one who performs) and the Word (the Scripture, the revealed will of God); James’s charge to obey, not merely hear.

📖 Biblical Definition

A doer of the word is one who not only hears the Scripture but obeys it, putting it into practice in his life. The phrase comes from the Epistle of James, which presses the point with great force: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” James likens the hearer who does not obey to a man beholding his natural face in a glass, who goes his way and straightway forgets what manner of man he was; but the doer, who looks into the perfect law of liberty and continues therein, is not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, and shall be blessed in his deed. The doctrine is not works-righteousness—James does not teach that obedience earns salvation—but the necessary fruit and evidence of a living faith, for faith without works is dead. The same Lord who said “Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” built His Sermon on the Mount to this conclusion: the wise man hears His sayings and does them, building on the rock, while the foolish hears and does them not, building on the sand. The dictionary holds the doctrine of the doer of the word as the test of genuine religion: hearing, even delighting in, the Word is not enough; saving faith works, obeys, and bears fruit, and the profession that does not issue in obedience is self-deception. The proof of having truly heard is doing.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

One who obeys the Scripture, not merely hears it—James’s charge to be doers of the word and not hearers only; obedience the necessary fruit and evidence of living faith.

DOER OF THE WORD, one who obeys the Scripture, not merely hears it.

“Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Hearing and approving the Word is mistaken for obeying it, and a fruitless profession is treated as living faith.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that hearing is not obeying. An age rich in sermons, books, podcasts, and conferences may grow vast in religious information while remaining barren of obedience—hearers only, deceiving their own selves. James and the Lord Jesus alike press the test: the proof of having heard is doing, and the profession that bears no fruit of obedience is dead and self-deceived.

The doctrine must be guarded on both sides. It is not works-righteousness; the doer is not justified by his doing, for justification is by faith alone. But the faith that justifies is never alone—it works, obeys, and bears fruit. To press obedience as the fruit and evidence of faith is not to deny grace but to honor it, for grace produces a changed and obedient life. The dictionary holds the doer of the word against both the antinomian who divorces faith from obedience and the legalist who makes obedience the ground of acceptance: faith alone justifies, but obedient doing proves the faith to be alive.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase names the obedient hearer, whose doing of the Word proves the reality of his faith.

expand to see more

Greek poiētēs — a doer, maker, performer; “doers of the word.”

Greek akroatēs — a hearer; the merely passive listener James warns against.

Greek logos — word; the Scripture, the revealed will of God.

The “perfect law of liberty” — the gospel law into which the doer looks and continues.

The doing is fruit and evidence of faith, not the ground of justification.

Usage

"“Doers of the word, and not hearers only” is preached against sermon-rich but fruitless religion."

"It is balanced to teach obedience as evidence, not ground, of justification."

"Christ’s wise and foolish builders illustrate hearing-and-doing versus hearing-only."
